Agadir is one of the major cities in Morocco, situated on the shore of the Atlantic near the foot of Atlas Mountains, and just north of the point where Sous River flows into the Atlantic Ocean. Agadir is at a distance of 508 kilometers to the south of Casablanca. It is also the capital of Agadir-Ida Ou Tanane Prefecture and of Souss-Massa economic region. The majority of Agadir's inhabitants speak Shilha as their first language (Berber language of Atlas branch). In 2012 the population of Agadir numbered 600,000 inhabitants.

In 1960 the city of Agadir was destroyed by an earthquake. Later on, it was completely recovered with mandatory seismic standards. Today it is Morocco's largest seaside resort, where foreign tourists and lots of residents are attracted by the mild year-round climate. Agadir has been well served by cheap flights and a motorway out of Tangier since 2010. 

Over the decades, the city has had several ports: a major trading port, two fishing ports, and the recent port with marina for leisure boats. Avenue du Port is the main artery of Anza district. It is surrounded by canneries and offers many small restaurants that are adjacent to the fish market. Agadir's fishing port is one of the world's premier major sardine ports. The commercial port is famous for its exports of manganese, zinc, cobalt and citrus products.

The economy of Agadir relies mainly on fisheries and tourism. Agricultural activities are based all around the city. Agadir boasts its Souk Al Ahad - one of the largest Souks in Morocco. The city also has its cement company named Ciments du Maroc (CIMAR), subsidiary of the Italian Italcementi. There is also a shipyard and Morocco's only Merchant Marine school.

Some of the prettiest beaches in Morocco lie to the north of Agadir. Areas known for excellent surfing are situated close to the village of Taghazout to Cap Ghir. Many smaller and beautiful beaches are located along this coast between Agadir and Essaouira.

Agadir is not a walk-off historic port. Cruise ships normally dock inside the working commercial port north of the resort center, where official port infrastructure includes berths used for cruise vessels. The main beach, marina and central sightseeing area are roughly 3–5 km (1.9–3.1 mi) from the cruise berths, depending on the berth and destination. For most passengers, a shuttle or taxi is the practical way to start sightseeing rather than walking through the port area.

Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport. Once you reach the marina, beach or city center, Agadir is straightforward to explore independently. A taxi is useful for combining the waterfront, Agadir Oufella and Souk El Had; organized transport is preferable for longer trips into the mountains or countryside.

Getting from the Cruise Port

  • Dock or tender: Cruise ships normally dock; Agadir is not generally a tender port.
  • Walking: Do not rely on walking directly from the ship. The berth is inside a large commercial port, pedestrian access can depend on port arrangements, and the route toward town is industrial rather than scenic.
  • Shuttles: Some cruise lines arrange transfers between the port and the tourist area. Availability and drop-off points vary by ship, so check the information provided onboard.
  • Taxis: Usually the simplest option for independent visitors, especially if visiting several sights. Confirm the fare or use the meter where applicable before setting off.
  • Public transport: Agadir has an extensive urban bus network, but stops accessible from a particular cruise berth are less predictable. For a short port call, taxis are normally more convenient.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Agadir Oufella, Cable Car and Waterfront

Allow: about 3–4 hours. Best for: first-time visitors.

Start with Agadir Oufella, the hilltop Kasbah overlooking the harbor and sweeping curve of Agadir Bay. The modern cable car provides an easy alternative to travelling up the hill by road; its route is approximately 1.7 km (1.1 mi) and the ride takes only a few minutes. After returning downhill, continue to the marina and Corniche for an easy waterfront walk.

This combination is practical independently using a taxi between the port and the lower cable-car/waterfront area. Check locally that the cable car is operating before committing your day to it.

Souk El Had and Central Agadir

Allow: about 2–3 hours for the market, or 3–4 hours combined with the waterfront. Best for: shopping, food and local atmosphere.

Souk El Had occupies more than 13 hectares and has thousands of stalls selling produce, spices, clothing, leather goods, household products and local specialties such as argan oil and amlou. Exploring independently is straightforward and a guide is not necessary.

The market is roughly 4.5 km (2.8 mi) from Agadir Marina. Walking between the two takes about an hour, so a taxi is usually a better choice during a cruise call. Souk El Had is normally closed on Mondays for weekly cleaning.

Agadir Beach and the Corniche

Allow: 2–4 hours. Best for: an easy, low-stress port day.

Agadir's broad sandy bay is the simplest option for passengers who do not want extensive sightseeing. Once transferred from the commercial port, the waterfront is easy to explore on foot. Combine time on the beach with the promenade and marina, leaving ample time for a taxi or shuttle back to the ship.

Taghazout

Allow: about 4–5 hours. Best for: coastal scenery, cafés and surf culture.

Taghazout is approximately 20 km (12.4 mi) north of Agadir. The former fishing village has a compact waterfront, beaches, cafés and surf shops. It is realistic during a normal-length port call using a pre-arranged driver, taxi or organized transfer.

Public transport is possible but less attractive for cruise passengers because waiting and connections reduce the safety margin for returning to the ship. If taking a surf lesson or travelling farther along the coast, arrange transport in advance.

Self-Guided Waterfront and City Walk

Marina to Souk El Had

Start: Agadir Marina after arriving from the cruise port by taxi or shuttle. Distance: approximately 4.5 km (2.8 mi). Pure walking time: about 1 hour. Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours including stops. Difficulty: Easy to moderate; mostly level urban walking.

  1. Agadir Marina – Walk around the yacht basin and waterfront before heading south.
  2. Agadir Corniche – Follow the broad seafront promenade with views across the bay toward Agadir Oufella.
  3. Agadir Beach – Continue beside the beach; this is the easiest section of the walk and can be shortened if the weather is hot.
  4. Place Al Amal area – Turn inland toward central Agadir.
  5. Jardin Ibn Zaidoun – Use the central garden area as a shaded pause on the way toward the market.
  6. Souk El Had – Finish with approximately 60–90 minutes in the market.

Rather than walking the same route back, take a taxi from Souk El Had directly to the cruise port or to your ship's confirmed shuttle point. In hot weather, reversing the itinerary and walking only part of the waterfront is more comfortable.

Longer Shore Excursions

Paradise Valley

Paradise Valley lies approximately 58 km (36.0 mi) from Agadir in the High Atlas foothills. The route includes winding mountain roads followed by walking through rocky terrain. Conditions at the pools and waterfalls vary considerably by season.

Organized excursion recommended. Although independent travel using buses and shared taxis is technically possible, connections can involve waiting and transport becomes less frequent later in the day. That makes public transport unsuitable for most cruise schedules. Allow roughly 5–6 hours for a comfortable visit and use proper footwear.

Taroudant

Taroudant is approximately 80 km (49.7 mi) from Agadir, generally around 1–1.5 hours each way by road. Its walled medina, traditional souks and ochre ramparts provide a more traditional old-city experience than modern Agadir.

Organized excursion or pre-arranged private driver recommended. The return journey consumes a substantial part of the port call, so this is best reserved for ships with a long day in Agadir. A visit combining Taroudant with additional distant attractions requires an especially generous schedule.

Practical Tips

  • Agadir was largely rebuilt after the 1960 earthquake, so do not expect a historic medina immediately outside the port. Agadir Oufella preserves the city's principal historic viewpoint, while the modern Medina Polizzi complex lies farther south.
  • For a short call, a taxi linking Agadir Oufella, the marina and Souk El Had is usually more time-efficient than relying on buses.
  • Carry Moroccan dirhams for markets and smaller purchases. Cash remains useful in Souk El Had.
  • The waterfront is flat and easy to walk, but heat and strong sun can make even moderate distances tiring.
  • Allow additional return time when travelling from Taghazout, Paradise Valley or Taroudant. Traffic, port security and shuttle arrangements can add time at the end of the day.
  • Confirm the ship's all-aboard time and any shuttle schedule before leaving the port, and keep a sensible margin for returning to the vessel.
